paragraphs: BOCLOAK studies whether social-media bot detectors based on graph neural networks remain effective against attackers operating under realistic constraints. The central concern is that feasible changes to a social network depend on domain rules and timing. Attacks that ignore these restrictions can give a misleading picture of detector robustness.

The framework represents neighboring accounts through a probability distribution over their spatial and temporal features. It learns an optimal-transport geometry that distinguishes human and bot behavior, then converts transport plans into sparse, plausible changes to connections. Its evaluation covers both editing edges and injecting nodes, with constraints built into the attack setting.

The experiments span three bot datasets, five detectors, three defenses, and four competing attack methods. BOCLOAK reports attack-success improvements of up to 80.13% while using 99.80% less GPU memory under the studied constraints. These results support optimal transport as a computationally lightweight way to test weaknesses in graph-based bot detection under more realistic attack conditions.
icml-2026-bocloak-optimal-transport-guid.tldr: BOCLOAK uses optimal transport to test graph-based bot detectors with realistic, constrained attacks that achieve higher success with much lower memory use.

paragraphs: Generating realistic tables becomes difficult when a single column mixes continuous measurements with discrete outcomes. A numerical feature may contain ordinary values alongside missing entries or unusually frequent special values. The paper addresses this within-feature mixture, which requires preserving more structure than simply distinguishing categorical columns from numerical ones.

Its generator proceeds in two stages. First, it creates a coarse version of a row containing categorical features and categorical summaries of numerical features. Those summaries explicitly represent discrete outcomes. A higher-resolution flow-matching model then uses the coarse row through a guided conditional probability path and data-dependent coupling to produce detailed numerical values.

The authors prove that this cascade tightens a transport-cost bound, giving theoretical support for the staged construction. Empirically, they report more realistic generated samples and better preservation of distributional details, including a 51.9% improvement in detection score. The approach matters because it makes exceptional numerical states part of the generation process rather than leaving them implicit in a continuous representation.
icml-2026-cascaded-flow-matching-for-het.tldr: A coarse-to-fine tabular generator explicitly models discrete outcomes within numerical features to improve sample realism.

paragraphs: This paper targets anomaly detection in streams with many measurement channels. Three problems motivate the design: mixer models can violate temporal ordering, unrelated channels can introduce misleading correlations, and isolated anomaly scores can overlook continuity over time. Together, these issues can produce noisy representations and inaccurate decisions about unusual behavior.

The proposed model groups channels according to their correlations and gives each group a dedicated embedding layer. A causal mixer combines information while respecting temporal causality, making the processing suitable for online use. This structure lets the model organize channel relationships before integrating their information, addressing the influence of spurious correlations.

A separate sequential scoring method accumulates evidence over time and refines where anomalies begin and end. Thus, both representation learning and the final detection process account for the structure of a continuing stream. Evaluations on six public benchmarks report consistently superior performance. The findings support combining channel grouping, causal processing, and temporally connected scoring for real-time multivariate anomaly detection.
icml-2026-cluster-aware-causal-mixer-for.tldr: A cluster-aware causal mixer combines channel grouping with sequential evidence accumulation to improve online time-series anomaly detection.

paragraphs: Physical behavior near singularities, interfaces, and critical points often follows power laws. Conventional neural networks can represent such behavior while leaving its governing exponents hidden inside their parameters. MSN-PINN makes those exponents explicit, allowing the model to return both a solution and an interpretable description of its scaling structure.

The network uses a power-law basis whose exponents are trainable. The authors establish conditions for unique recovery and provide a conditional squared-error scaling result for the learned exponents. Training also incorporates physical constraints, including compatibility with boundary conditions, so the search for scaling behavior respects requirements of the underlying problem.

Experiments recover individual exponents with 1–5% error under noisy and sparse observations. More specialized tests report 0.009% error for Laplace corner singularities and 0.03% and 0.05% errors for singular Poisson problems. A 40-configuration wedge benchmark achieves complete success with 0.022% mean error. Constraint-aware training improves accuracy by three orders of magnitude over naive training, emphasizing the value of encoding physical requirements.
icml-2026-discovering-scaling-exponents-.tldr: MSN-PINN learns physical scaling exponents explicitly alongside solutions, with conditional recovery guarantees and strong experimental accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper questions whether optimizer choices inherited from language-model pretraining and supervised fine-tuning are equally suitable for reinforcement learning. AdamW is widely used for large Transformers but carries substantial memory overhead. The authors investigate whether its momentum and adaptive learning rates provide the same value when models learn from rewards.

Their analysis finds that both mechanisms influence reinforcement learning less than supervised fine-tuning. This motivates testing the simpler, more memory-efficient stochastic gradient descent optimizer. In the reported language-model reinforcement-learning experiments, SGD matches or exceeds AdamW, despite its known difficulties in supervised training of large Transformers.

The updates also exhibit striking sparsity: full fine-tuning with SGD changes fewer than 0.02% of the model, over 1,000 times fewer parameters than AdamW, without regularization designed to encourage sparsity. The paper offers possible explanations for this behavior. These findings suggest that reinforcement learning can use substantially fewer effective parameter updates than previously recognized, while showing that optimizer effectiveness depends on the training objective.
icml-2026-do-we-need-adam-surprisingly-s.tldr: In the reported LLM reinforcement-learning experiments, SGD matches or outperforms AdamW while producing much sparser updates and reducing optimizer memory needs.

paragraphs: DRIFT addresses training language models to improve through multiple rounds of interaction and lightweight feedback. Online reinforcement learning can account for these evolving conversations, but repeatedly generating complete correction trajectories is expensive. Ordinary offline supervised fine-tuning is simpler, yet can suffer from distribution shift and collapse in the behavior it learns.

The method builds on an equivalence between a KL-regularized reinforcement-learning objective and importance-weighted supervised learning. It first collects interaction trajectories using a fixed reference policy. It then derives weights from their returns and trains the target policy with weighted supervised fine-tuning, separating trajectory generation from the optimization process.

This separation allows the training procedure to use reward information across interactions without generating fresh correction trajectories at every update. In the reported experiments, DRIFT matches or exceeds multi-turn reinforcement-learning baselines while retaining the efficiency and simplicity associated with supervised fine-tuning. The result supports weighted offline training as an effective approach to multi-turn optimization in the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-drift-decoupled-rollouts-and-i.tldr: DRIFT trains on return-weighted offline interaction trajectories to achieve competitive multi-turn behavior with supervised-fine-tuning efficiency.

paragraphs: Federated learning becomes harder when clients hold data from substantially different domains. Sharing one representative point for each class can help coordinate training, but a single point loses the shape of a class distribution. FML instead transfers geometric structure, aiming to retain information about how examples within a class are organized.

Clients send compressed representations of class manifolds: the intrinsic structures their features form. An attention-based mechanism on the server adaptively combines these representations and lets structures from different domains inform one another. The resulting global target is intended to unify learning while retaining flexibility across client domains.

Local training follows this shared structure through a manifold approximation loss and a separation loss. These objectives connect each client's model to the global geometry while maintaining distinctions between classes. Experiments on Digits and Office31 report improvements of up to 6.47% in accuracy over state-of-the-art methods. The results support richer structural communication as a way to address domain differences that class prototypes oversimplify.
icml-2026-federated-manifold-learning-fm.tldr: FML shares and combines class geometry across federated clients to improve learning when their data domains differ.

paragraphs: Flowers are neural models for learning the operators that produce solutions to partial differential equations. Their main building block is a multihead warp: each head predicts a displacement and samples input features at the resulting source coordinate. This makes adaptive movement through the feature field the basis of information exchange.

Displacements are predicted pointwise, without aggregating spatial neighborhoods. Each head obtains nonlocal information through one source sample, and stacked multiscale residual blocks build global interactions at linear cost. The architecture also uses pointwise channel mixing and a multiscale scaffold. The authors motivate the design through conservation-law flow maps, waves in varying media, and a kinetic-theoretic continuum limit.

On two- and three-dimensional time-dependent PDE benchmarks, particularly flows and waves, a 17-million-parameter model consistently beats similarly sized Fourier, convolutional, and attention-based alternatives. A 150-million-parameter version also improves on recent Transformer foundation models using more parameters, data, and compute. These comparisons support sparse adaptive warping as an effective architecture for the evaluated physical solution operators.
icml-2026-flowers-a-warp-drive-for-neura.tldr: Flowers learn PDE solution operators through sparse adaptive warps, delivering strong benchmark performance with linear-cost global interactions.

paragraphs: GUDA asks which groups of training examples influenced a diffusion model's generated image. Groups might represent artistic styles or object classes. The question is counterfactual: how would the model's behavior on that image change if a particular group had been absent from training? Answering it directly by repeated retraining becomes expensive as group counts grow.

The method starts from one model trained on all the data and applies machine unlearning separately for each group. These unlearned models approximate the models that would result from leaving groups out. GUDA measures influence through changes in an ELBO-based likelihood score between the full model and each approximate counterfactual.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and artistic-style attribution with Stable Diffusion find more reliable identification of primary contributing groups than semantic similarity, gradient-based attribution, and instance-level unlearning. On CIFAR-10, it achieves roughly a hundredfold speedup over leave-one-group-out retraining. The contribution is a practical approximation to group-removal attribution that directly examines model behavior under unlearning.
icml-2026-guda-counterfactual-group-wise.tldr: GUDA uses group unlearning to approximate counterfactual training-data attribution for diffusion models much faster than repeated retraining.

paragraphs: Model predictive control chooses actions by forecasting trajectories and solving an optimization problem. Nonlinear dynamics, safety constraints, and numerical computation can make individual choices difficult for operators to understand. Hierarchical Causal Abduction combines several kinds of evidence to explain why a nonlinear controller selected a particular action.

The framework brings together physics-informed domain knowledge graphs, optimization evidence from KKT multipliers, and temporal causal discovery using PCMCI. These provide complementary views of the physical system, the optimization process, and relationships over time. HCA ranks and validates explanations using this combined evidence, aiming for interpretations faithful to the controller's decisions.

Across greenhouse climate, building HVAC, and chemical-process applications with expert validation, shared parameters yield explanation accuracy of 0.478 versus LIME's 0.311, a 53% improvement. Domain-specific KKT-threshold calibration over two to three days raises accuracy to 0.88. Removing any evidence source lowers accuracy by 32–37%. The paper also reports applicability of its ranking-and-validation methodology beyond MPC, including learning-based control and trajectory planning.
icml-2026-hierarchical-causal-abduction-.tldr: HCA combines physical knowledge, optimization evidence, and temporal causal discovery to explain model-predictive-control actions more accurately.

paragraphs: This paper studies chain of thought through a classification view of language tasks. A model receives a prompt and selects among possible answers. The authors show that classification error scales as a power law with the number of answer classes, connecting the difficulty of a decision to the size of its choice set.

They model reasoning as a tree that splits one large classification problem into a sequence of smaller ones. Each step has the same number of choices, called the degree. Increasing tree depth represents taking more reasoning steps. Within this formulation, decomposition can substantially reduce prediction error by changing the size and sequence of the decisions the model makes.

The benefit depends on degree: below a critical threshold, additional thinking is detrimental. Above that threshold, an optimal depth minimizes error, and greater depth cannot surpass that minimum. The result gives a conditional account of when longer reasoning helps and identifies a limit to improvement from depth alone within the proposed model.
icml-2026-how-does-chain-of-thought-deco.tldr: A classification-tree model of chain of thought identifies when decomposition helps and why increasing reasoning depth eventually stops improving error.

paragraphs: WiFi-Mamba estimates three-dimensional human poses from WiFi channel information, including scenes with multiple people. The paper targets the quadratic complexity of Transformer approaches and their lack of explicit structure for the signal's physical properties. WiFi sensing offers a setting for privacy-preserving monitoring that remains useful under visual occlusion.

The architecture processes signal amplitude and phase through separate selective state-space streams, with coupling between their internal states. This respects the distinct physical roles of the two inputs while allowing them to exchange information. A selective state attention mechanism decodes pose queries using sequential context, and persistent state-space memory supports consistency between frames without recurrent memory explosion.

On the Person-in-WiFi 3D dataset, experiments covering different person counts report a 16–27% reduction in mean per-joint position error. The model uses 2.14 million parameters versus the baseline's 48.2 million, or 4.4% as many. These results demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off in the evaluated setting and support potential use in continuous monitoring on edge devices.
icml-2026-interleaved-selective-state-sp.tldr: WiFi-Mamba uses coupled state-space streams and persistent memory to improve WiFi-based 3D pose estimation with far fewer parameters.

paragraphs: ITSPACE addresses alignment of feature distributions summarized by covariance matrices. Under a centered Gaussian approximation, the unregularized Wasserstein-2 transport discrepancy becomes a closed-form covariance objective called the Bures–Wasserstein objective. The method directly optimizes this quantity, making the distributional approximation central to the meaning of the alignment.

Its proximal majorization-minimization procedure uses closed-form updates in a square-root factorization. In exact arithmetic, every iteration satisfies a sufficient-decrease inequality for the objective. For inexact polar computations, the authors provide an explicit bound controlling deviations from exact descent. The factorization preserves positive-semidefinite structure by construction and accommodates restricted-rank representations.

These properties make the procedure suitable as a small inner optimization loop when unlabeled target batches must support adaptation under limited computation and few steps. Across real-world covariance-alignment benchmarks, ITSPACE reaches low objective gaps substantially faster than Bures–Wasserstein gradient descent, alternative covariance geometries, and regularized sample-transport baselines. Its contribution combines efficient empirical alignment with carefully qualified guarantees about objective descent.
icml-2026-itspace-monotone-gaussian-opti.tldr: ITSPACE efficiently aligns covariance representations through structure-preserving updates with exact-arithmetic descent guarantees and bounds for inexact computation.

paragraphs: LAPRAS studies how predictions about future database queries can improve differentially private answers under one global privacy budget. Recurring jobs make query identities potentially predictable even when their arrival order is unknown. The formal setting assumes a stream of linear queries arriving in uniformly random order and an oracle supplying a predicted query set.

The algorithm allocates privacy spending through two routes. Predicted queries use the offline-optimal Matrix Mechanism, while unexpected queries draw on a residual budget through online answering. This division lets useful predictions inform the overall allocation while retaining resources for queries that the oracle missed.

To handle the unknown number of unexpected queries, Smooth Allocation builds an unbiased stopping-time estimate from the first number of such queries proportional to the squared logarithm of stream size. It then continually adjusts per-query expenditure. Experiments on two real datasets show near-offline utility when predictions overlap strongly with the stream and graceful degradation toward baseline performance when overlap is low.
icml-2026-lapras-learning-augmented-priv.tldr: LAPRAS uses predicted query sets to allocate a global privacy budget while adapting spending to unexpected queries.

paragraphs: CrysLDNet addresses a mismatch in materials modeling: predicting crystal properties requires useful structural representations, but labeled property data are scarce. The paper uses pretraining on large amounts of unlabeled crystal data so that a graph encoder can learn structural and chemical information before being adapted to a particular prediction task.

The pretraining framework combines a variational autoencoder with a diffusion model. The autoencoder maps three-dimensional crystal structures into a smooth latent space, and diffusion operates within that representation. The resulting graph encoder is then fine-tuned for property prediction, connecting generative representation learning to the supervised task.

Experiments on density-functional-theory datasets report significant gains over both training from scratch and pretrained alternatives, including improvements of 4.26% on JARVIS and 4.90% on MP. The learned representations also remain robust with sparse data. When fine-tuned using limited experimental observations, they can correct DFT errors. These findings support latent diffusion pretraining as a way to make scarce labeled and experimental crystal data more useful.
icml-2026-latent-diffusion-pretraining-f.tldr: CrysLDNet pretrains crystal representations with latent diffusion to improve property prediction when labeled data are scarce.

paragraphs: Repeated time-series measurements often carry several categories of metadata. A neuroscience trial, for example, might have labels for task difficulty and animal choice. MILCCI aims to separate how these different label categories appear in the recorded signals while also describing variation between trials and the interpretable components underlying the observations.

The method extends a sparse decomposition performed for each trial. It uses similarities between labels within each category to guide subtle adjustments in component composition across trials. This allows related trials to inform one another while helping distinguish the contribution associated with each metadata category.

MILCCI also learns a temporal trace for each component. These traces evolve within trials and can vary flexibly between trials, so the representation captures both component composition and changing temporal behavior. Demonstrations include synthetic data, voting patterns, online page-view trends, and neuronal recordings. Together, these examples show how the method combines multiple label categories with trial-specific dynamics to support interpretation across different kinds of temporal data.
icml-2026-multi-integration-of-labels-ac.tldr: MILCCI uses multiple metadata categories to disentangle interpretable components and trial-specific dynamics in repeated time-series measurements.

paragraphs: LoRA reduces fine-tuning costs by learning two adapter matrices whose product represents a low-rank parameter change. Its practical simplicity hides a theoretical difficulty: the resulting optimization problem lacks the Lipschitz smoothness used in standard convergence proofs. Earlier analyses therefore focused on limiting behavior or imposed strong boundedness assumptions to restore that condition.

This paper analyzes the original LoRA gradient-descent algorithm without those artificial boundedness assumptions. The proof reformulates the problem using the outer product of stacked adapter matrices. It then develops a modified descent lemma for the reparameterized objective's Lipschitz-like behavior and controls the step size to establish progress.

The result is a non-asymptotic convergence rate of O(1/log T) toward a stationary point after T iterations. This ties the guarantee to a finite iteration count rather than only describing eventual behavior. The contribution is a convergence analysis of the algorithm used in practice; the stated endpoint is stationarity, so the guarantee concerns reaching a point with vanishing first-order improvement.
icml-2026-on-the-convergence-rate-of-lor.tldr: The paper proves an O(1/log T) stationary-point convergence rate for original LoRA gradient descent without strong boundedness assumptions.

paragraphs: Static conditional value-at-risk evaluates the unfavorable tail of returns, making it useful when rare catastrophic outcomes matter. Its dependence on complete trajectories creates a challenge for reinforcement learning: the objective does not decompose through the ordinary Bellman recursion on the original state space. Classical approaches add a continuous state variable to restore a workable formulation.

The paper proposes a different augmented-state formulation that redistributes rewards across steps. Its Bellman operator provides dense per-step rewards and contraction properties across the full space of bounded value functions. This addresses sparse rewards and degenerate fixed points that arise in the classical formulation unless value functions are restricted to a specialized admissible class.

The authors build risk-averse value iteration and model-free Q-learning on this foundation, using discretized augmented states. They provide convergence guarantees and bounds on the approximation error introduced by discretization. Empirical results show learning of CVaR-sensitive policies with effective performance-safety trade-offs, linking the theoretical reformulation to algorithms that account for unfavorable trajectory outcomes.
icml-2026-reward-redistribution-for-cvar.tldr: A new augmented-state CVaR formulation supplies dense rewards and contraction properties for convergent risk-averse learning algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper examines how architecture and scale affect foundation models trained on metagenomic sequences. It presents the methodology behind EDEN, a model family reaching 28 billion parameters and trained on 9.7 trillion nucleotide tokens. The goal is to identify effective ways to model the large and diverse sequence distribution found in metagenomic data.

The study compares autoregressive Llama-style Transformers, Mamba state-space models, and Hyena long-convolution models at nucleotide resolution. As capacity increases, the reported results favor the Llama architecture in scaling efficiency and semantic retrieval. This provides empirical evidence about architecture choice for this setting, where linear-time sequence models have attracted interest for long-range biological modeling.

The authors also derive quality-aware scaling laws showing predictable power-law behavior over three orders of magnitude in parameter and data scales. Evaluations cover unsupervised zero-shot fitness prediction, semantic completion, and gene recovery. Together, these findings offer an empirical guide for allocating scale and choosing architectures, with Transformers defining the frontier demonstrated in the study.
icml-2026-scaling-laws-and-architectural.tldr: An empirical study of EDEN finds favorable Transformer scaling for metagenomic modeling and derives quality-aware power-law relationships.

paragraphs: SINQ addresses quality loss when language-model weights are compressed to low precision, especially at four bits or fewer. Large outlier weights can force shared quantization scales that represent other weights poorly. This is particularly troublesome for uniform quantization methods that operate without calibration data.

The method adds a scale factor along a second matrix axis. A fast Sinkhorn–Knopp-style procedure finds row and column scales that normalize their variances. The authors show that weight-matrix structure reveals column scales predictive of typical training-time activation magnitudes, allowing the procedure to approximate activation-aware quantization without requiring those activations for calibration.

Each linear layer can be processed independently, simplifying application to new architectures. Evaluations including the Qwen3 family report reductions of more than 50% in the perplexity gap on WikiText2 and C4 relative to uncalibrated uniform baselines, with zero to negligible computational overhead. Combining SINQ with calibration or nonuniform quantization can improve it further. The findings show that weight structure itself can guide better low-precision scaling.
icml-2026-sinq-sinkhorn-normalized-quant.tldr: SINQ normalizes weight matrices along both axes to improve calibration-free low-precision quantization with negligible overhead.

paragraphs: Terminal embeddings reduce dimension while preserving distances from every point in a chosen dataset to any possible query point. This supports small weighted summaries, called coresets, whose clustering costs approximate those of the full dataset for every candidate solution. Extending this idea to time series is difficult because straight-line interpolation between measurements introduces structure that ordinary terminal embeddings do not directly preserve.

The paper generalizes terminal embeddings to affine line segments. This overcomes the mismatch between nonlinear terminal mappings and the linear pieces used to represent time-series curves. The resulting construction supports dimension reduction while respecting the segments relevant to these time-series representations.

Using this approach, the authors obtain the first dimension-free coresets for time-series clustering under Fréchet distance. Their dimension-reduction procedure relies on Johnson–Lindenstrauss embeddings, and experiments on real-world time series compare favorably with PCA. The theoretical contribution extends a powerful compression technique from individual points to structured curves, while the experiments indicate practical promise for the underlying reduction.
icml-2026-terminal-dimension-reduction-f.tldr: Line-segment-preserving terminal embeddings enable the first dimension-free coresets for time-series clustering under Fréchet distance.

paragraphs: Time-PEFT addresses how to recognize time-series datasets likely to benefit from fine-tuning a foundation model. Existing approaches adapt models without a clear criterion for identifying difficult datasets where zero-shot forecasts deteriorate. The paper introduces two data-derived complexity measures to connect dataset characteristics with potential gains from adaptation.

Temporal complexity uses spectral entropy in the frequency domain to quantify how difficult it is to identify distinct patterns. Multichannel complexity measures information flow between channels that can affect predictive uncertainty. The authors present these measures as useful proxies for fine-tuning gains, providing a way to characterize challenges beyond standard benchmark settings.

The resulting framework adds a frequency adapter with top-k filtering and a channel adapter for modeling relationships across channels. These components address the two forms of complexity within a parameter-efficient adaptation scheme. Using the base MOMENT model as its backbone, Time-PEFT improves performance by up to 38% over LoRA on complex datasets, supporting the value of tailoring adaptation to temporal and cross-channel structure.
icml-2026-time-peft-temporal-and-multich.tldr: Time-PEFT uses temporal and cross-channel complexity measures to motivate targeted adapters that improve forecasting on complex datasets.

paragraphs: UrbanFusion learns spatial representations intended to support different urban prediction tasks, including housing prices and public-health indicators. Such tasks draw on varied geospatial inputs, but generic spatial models often handle only a limited range of modalities or lack a mechanism for combining them. The paper addresses both representation breadth and multimodal integration.

Separate encoders process street-view images, remote-sensing data, cartographic maps, and points of interest. A Transformer fusion module combines their outputs into a unified location representation. The stochastic multimodal framework can use any available subset of these inputs during both pretraining and inference, accommodating differences in what data exist for each location.

Evaluation spans 41 tasks across 56 cities worldwide. The authors report stronger location encoding and predictive performance than prior GeoAI models, together with good generalization to regions absent from training. These findings support a reusable spatial representation that can combine multiple views of a location while remaining usable when only some modalities are available.
icml-2026-urbanfusion-stochastic-multimo.tldr: UrbanFusion combines flexible subsets of geospatial modalities into spatial representations that generalize across urban tasks and unseen regions.

paragraphs: The curse of depth describes language models whose later layers contribute less than earlier ones. The paper connects this underuse to accumulated variance growth in pre-layer-normalized models, which can push deep blocks toward behavior that barely changes their inputs. It investigates whether mechanisms resembling sparsity can dampen that growth and improve layer utilization.

The study covers sparsity emerging through training and inputs, including weight decay and long-context attention, as well as architectural mechanisms such as shared keys and values in grouped-query attention and selective expert activation. Controlled depth-scaling experiments and targeted interventions on layer effectiveness examine how these choices relate to variance and layer differentiation.

Across the studied settings, reduced effective interaction density tends to accompany lower output variance and more differentiated layers. The authors turn these observations into a practical training recipe that yields a reported 4.6 accuracy improvement on downstream tasks. The evidence suggests that sparsity-related choices deserve attention in depth scaling, while the central relationship remains empirically qualified rather than universal.
icml-2026-when-does-sparsity-mitigate-th.tldr: Experiments link sparsity-like mechanisms to lower variance growth and better use of deep LLM layers, informing an effective training recipe.

paragraphs: Group Relative Policy Optimization trains reasoning models by comparing sampled trajectories within a group. Extended deliberation can create more opportunities for relative gains, encouraging inefficient continuation. A blanket length penalty is difficult to tune because hard problems may genuinely require longer reasoning, and final-answer correctness usually supplies no direct labels for when to stop.

WS-GRPO turns those final correctness outcomes into guidance for partially completed trajectories. It trains a preference model from outcome-only supervision to produce signals about whether further continuation is beneficial. This provides correctness-aware continue-or-stop guidance at intermediate prefixes without requiring explicit stopping annotations.

The method therefore aims to distinguish useful additional reasoning from redundant deliberation rather than applying the same token penalty everywhere. The paper provides theoretical results and evaluates the approach on reasoning benchmarks. Reported experiments substantially shorten rollouts while maintaining accuracy competitive with GRPO baselines. The contribution is a way to extract intermediate efficiency guidance from the outcome supervision already available for reasoning training.
icml-2026-ws-grpo-weakly-supervised-grou.tldr: WS-GRPO converts final-answer correctness into intermediate stopping guidance to shorten reasoning rollouts while preserving competitive accuracy.
